name: Moral Credential Effect
description: After establishing themselves as moral, fair, or non-prejudiced, people may feel more permitted to act in a less ethical or less egalitarian way afterward. Prior virtue gets interpreted as a license.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to fairness/governance work, trust-and-safety decisions, ethics review, and product strategy: one conspicuous 'good' action can make a team or decision-maker feel licensed to relax later scrutiny or justify a questionable call.
myth_risk_note: Existing corpus already flags this as disputed: Monin & Miller (2001) introduced the specific credentialing effect, but a preregistered direct replication found near-zero effects. Mullen & Monin's (2015) Annual Review is directly on point here too: they note many studies in this literature lacked proper baseline conditions ('donut designs'), leaving licensing effects genuinely ambiguous, and found little evidence of BOTH consistency and licensing operating within the same study -- a real methodological complication, not just a discovery-pass artifact.
prevalence_note: Known in ethics, prejudice, behavioral-design, and organizational-psychology discussions, but not part of the most routine mainstream UX heuristic canon.

findings.description: Across three experiments, participants who had first established credentials as nonprejudiced were subsequently more willing to express later preferences or opinions that could be interpreted as prejudiced or politically incorrect — the classic moral credential effect.
findings.source_title: Moral credentials and the expression of prejudice.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

findings.description: In a preregistered direct replication of Monin and Miller's key moral-credentials paradigm (n = 932 after exclusions), the moral credential effect was near zero for ethnicity judgments and reversed for gender judgments, yielding no consistent support for the original effect.
findings.source_title: Licensing via Credentials: Replication Registered Report of Monin and Miller (2001) with Extensions Investigating the Domain-Specificity of Moral Credentials and the Association Between the Credential Effect and Trait Reputational Concern
